newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook-Diesel to maintain recovery.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook-Diesel to maintain recovery.

text.p: Asian middle distillate market was set to sustain its recovery with support from Indonesia and emerging demand from China after Hong Kong's handover, while the arbitrage from the west remained shut, traders said on Monday.
Diesel prices have hit a near-term floor of $21.50 per barrel during mid June but rebounded as buyers emerged to take advantage of cheap oil, traders said.
They said the surplus diesel supplies that flooded the market in the past weeks have gradually been absorbed.
But they also noted that spot prices could remain soft as long as the two sellers, who have been offering at low levels over the past week, continued to do so this week.
Nevertheless, traders said demand from Indonesia and firmer buying interest from China could prop diesel values.
Indonesia's state oil company Pertamina was expected to shut its 200,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) crude unit at the Balikpapan refinery for maintenance from July 10 for 32 days.
Another shutdown was due in August at a 100,000-bpd crude unit at the Cilacap facility for 35 days.

The archipelago was said to have taken about five million barrels of gas oil in July and was expected to import the same volume in August. This was about one million barrels above their normal monthly imports.
Pertamina was also likely to absorb up to three million barrels of jet fuel in July and the same volume in August due to the refinery shutdowns.
Indonesia's firm jet fuel demand has also caused the jet/gas oil spread to widen over the past two weeks.
Traders said China's diesel demand was expected to return to normal after Hong Kong's handover to the mainland at midnight on June 30.
In the past month, imports have been sporadic, distracted by the preparations for the handover, as security around the ports tightened, traders said.
"China will come out sooner or later, it cannot depend on its inventories to satisfy demand forever," said one trader.
China halved its April imports over March to about 400,000 tonnes and this volume was expected to remain in May. China's normal monthly imports were around 600,000-800,000 tonnes.
Traders also said they expected smuggling activities to pick up after the handover as the Chinese authorities eased their current tough crackdown.
A volatile fuel oil market have placed some uncertainties on the outlook of prices. Prices dropped to a mid-week low of $98 per tonne but rose later in the week to $100.
Demand from China is expected to provide support this week, traders said.
The low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR) market was still awaiting allocation details from Indonesia's Pertamina, which has initially decided to allot 2.3 million barrels in July, traders said.
Indonesia's refinery shutdowns have cut its LSWR output in July, they said.
Pertamina allocated 3.1 million barrels in June, with an additional 500,000 barrels rolled over from May.
"In any case, LSWR prices will just go up," said one trader, noting increasing summer demand from Japan.
Light distillates prices were in their doldrums. Traders said
unless fresh demand surfaced, prices would remain depressed.
There were still no signs of Indonesian gasoline demand, which some traders assessed at around 500,000 barrels a month in July and August on the back of refinery turnarounds.
But other market sources said Pertamina might draw from domestic stocks with additional supplies coming from the Balongan refinery during the shutdown period.
Sri Lanka's tender to sell 125,000 barrels of light naphtha for July 18-19 lifting will close on July 2 with validity until July 4.
Shell Singapore is also expected to maintain lower output at its 435,000-bpd refinery. Shell is currently producing at about 58,000 bpd, down from its normal 59,000 bpd.
Traders said the reduced output, although marginal, would provide some support for prices across the barrel.
